title: The Medium Is the Message
author: Dylan Kane
summary: Dylan Kane applies Marshall McLuhan's 'the medium is the message' to classroom technology, arguing that screens are not neutral delivery vehicles but shape student behavior in ways that undermine learning. Drawing on his own math-fact practice website, Kane coins the term 'videogamification' to describe how students transfer video-game completion habits to any screen-based learning task, prioritizing getting through over actually learning. Students on his website would deliberately answer early questions incorrectly to make subsequent questions easier—a behavior Kane ultimately addressed by replacing the website with a paper-and-pencil system. He pushes back against the 'instructional design inside the carrier is what matters' argument, noting that comprehension is robustly stronger when reading happens on paper than on screens—a property of the medium, not the content. The piece acknowledges that AI-monitored screens could achieve real accountability, but asks what kind of world and what kind of relationships that system prepares students for. Kane calls for honest conversation about tradeoffs rather than assuming technology is neutral or inherently superior to traditional tools.
points: 'Videogamification' describes how students bring video-game completion habits (find the path of least resistance, get through the task) to any screen-based learning activity, regardless of how good the underlying instructional design is.

Research consistently shows that reading comprehension is stronger on paper than on screens—Kane identifies this as a fundamental property of the medium, not a problem fixable through better content or instructional design.

The accountability argument for AI-monitored screens is real, but Kane asks: accountability from artificial intelligence sends a different message than accountability from a caring human teacher—a distinction that matters for what kind of people students become.
quotes: The basic idea is to adapt to the learner. The website tries to figure out which facts the student needs help with and gives them focused practice on those facts.
In a video game, the goal is to beat the level as quickly as possible, not to learn along the way. Students bring those habits with them when screens come out in math class.

students would deliberately get early questions wrong in order to give themselves an easier path through the task. I tried lots of stuff to mitigate this, but I kept running into the same fundamental problem: students were trying to get through the task, not trying to learn.

A wide range of studies have found that comprehension is stronger when reading happens on paper compared with a screen. This is a fundamental property of the medium: humans skim and struggle to attend deeply when reading on screens.
Accountability from artificial intelligence is different than accountability from a human. What message does that send to students? What kind of life does it prepare them for?
